papers.full_text: 1 Comparative transcriptomic response of bank vole kidney and respiratory 1 epithelial cells to distinct orthohantaviruses 2 Karine Badonnel 1,2, Thomas Cokelaer 3,4, Elodie Turc 5, Marc Monot 4,5, Jean Claude 3 Manuguerra 6, Myriam Ermonval 6#, and Giulia Gallo 7*#. 4 5 1 Université Paris-Saclay, UVSQ, INRAE, BREED, 78350, Jouy-en-Josas, France 6 2 Ecole Nationale Vétérinaire d’Alfort, BREED, 94700, Maisons-Alfort, France 7 3 Institut Pasteur, Université Paris Cité, Parasitologie Moléculaire et Signalisation, F-75015 Paris, 8 France 9 4 Institut Pasteur, Université Paris Cité, Bioinformatics and Biostatistics Hub, F-75015 Paris, France 10 5 Institut Pasteur, Université Paris Cité, Plate-forme Technologique Biomics, F-75015, Paris, France 11 6 Institut Pasteur, Université Paris Cité, Environnement et Risques Infectieux, F-75015 Paris, France 12 7 The Pirbright Institute, Woking, United Kingdom 13 14 *Corresponding author: 15 Giulia.Gallo@pirbright.ac.uk (GG) 16 # Equally contributed to the work 17 18 19 Short tittle: response of bank vole cells to orthohantaviruses 20 21 Keywords: orthohantaviruses, Puumala virus, Tula virus, Prospect Hill virus, 22 transcriptomic analysis, bank vole cells, RNA-seq 23 24 25 Data availability 26 The RNA-seq data set 2 and 3 generated as part of this work were deposited to ENA 27 (accession E-MTAB-16656). 28 2 Abstract 29 Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses distributed worldwide that can cause 30 diseases of varying severity in humans following occasional aerosol transmission. 31 While infections remain asymptomatic in their natural small-mammal reservoirs, 32 hantaviral pathogenesis in humans is associated with an exacerbated immune 33 response. The increasing number of outbreaks in endemic regions caused by the 34 modification of rodent habitats due to human activities and the risks of reassortments 35 in areas where multiple orthohantaviruses co-circulate with their animal reservoirs, 36 are of public health concern. These challenges highlight the need to better 37 understand how these viruses interact with host cells to spread within and between 38 organisms, and how antiviral responses are regulated, particularly in their natural 39 hosts. We previously showed that cellular susceptibility to orthohantaviruses depends 40 on both cell type and virus species and correlates with cellular restrictions acting at 41 different stages of the viral cycle. Here, we performed a comparative RNA- 42 sequencing study and transcriptomic analysis of the cellular responses induced by 43 three different orthohantaviruses in kidneys and respiratory tract cells derived from 44 bank voles, the natural host of an orthohantavirus pathogenic to humans. 45 Transcriptomic analyses revealed common as well as virus- and tissue-specific 46 regulatory pathways that may underlie distinct infection outcomes. It highlighted the 47 complexity of viral interactions with bank vole at a cellular level, including innate 48 immune responses and antiviral signaling pathways. 49 50 Introduction 51 Orthohantaviruses (1) are found in small mammals, such as rodents, shrews, moles 52 and bats. Their long co-evolution with these globally distributed host species (2-4) 53 3 accounts for their presence in all continents (5). These viruses do not cause apparent 54 diseases in their natural hosts. Currently, only rodent-borne orthohantaviruses are 55 known to be pathogenic in humans, mainly through the inhalation of aerosols from 56 contaminated animal excreta. After entering the respiratory tract, orthohantaviruses 57 cross the pulmonary epithelial barrier and disseminate throughout the body by 58 infecting vascular endothelial cells and monocytes (6, 7). In humans, an exacerbated 59 immune response (8) leads to hemorrhagic fevers with renal syndromes (HFRS) and 60 nephropathia epidemica (NE) in the Old World (9), or to hantavirus cardio-pulmonary 61 syndromes (HCPS) in the Americas (10). The activation of innate immunity to 62 eliminate viruses, and the viral strategies to counteract it, vary depending on the 63 orthohantavirus species (11). Sustained interferon (IFN) activation may contribute to 64 inflammatory responses that influence viral pathogenicity (12). 65 We previously showed that the pathogenic Puumala virus (PUUV), the weakly 66 pathogenic Tula virus (TULV) and the non-pathogenic Prospect Hill virus (PHV), 67 differentially regulate IFN responses in human and rodent cells (13, 14). Myodes 68 glareolus (bank vole) is the natural host of PUUV, whereas TULV and PHV naturally 69 infect Microtus arvalis (common vole) and Microtus pensylvanicus (eastern meadow 70 vole), respectively. These orthohantaviruses exhibit different replication 71 characteristics in bank voles-derived cells. These differences correlate with cellular 72 restrictions acting at distinct stages of the viral cycle from entry to replication and viral 73 release (14). In human cells, type I and III IFNs and several IFN stimulated genes 74 (ISGs) are strongly activated by PUUV and PHV but not by TULV. In contrast, bank 75 vole cells display a delayed and weaker IFN response. 76 Despite advances in our understanding of the regulation of host responses in 77 rodents, the mechanisms leading to the differential outcomes of orthohantavirus 78 4 infection in their natural hosts remain poorly understood (15-18). To explore this 79 question, we compared gene expression profiles induced by PUUV, TULV and PHV. 80 Building on the opportunity that the recent availability of an updated Myodes 81 glareolus genome assembly in the NCBI database (GCF_902806735.1) provides, we 82 performed transcriptomic analysis by RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of bank vole 83 epithelial cells derived from the kidneys (MyglaSWRecB) and the respiratory tract 84 (MyglaSWTrach and MyglaAEC#2) infected with these different orthohantaviruses. 85 Differential gene expression and pathway analyses revealed virus- and tissue- 86 specific regulatory programs that likely contribute to distinct infection outcomes and 87 host–virus interactions. 88 89 Material and methods 90 Cells and viruses 91 The three bank vole cells lines, MyglaSWRecB, MyglaSWTrach, MyglaAEC, 92 originated from kidney, tracheal and alveolar lung epithelium, respectively, and were 93 SV40 T antigen-immortalized (19). Cells were grown at 37°C with 5% CO2 in DMEM 94 medium (Gibco) supplemented with 10% of heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum 95 (Biosera). 96 Puumala Sotkamo viral strain (PUUV) and Prospect Hill viral strain (PHV) were 97 provided by Andreas Rang (Charité University, Berlin). Tula Moravia virus (TULV) 98 was obtained from Alexander Plyusnin (Helsinki University). Viral stocks were 99 propagated on Vero E6 cells as previously described (14). 100 RNA preparation, sequencing and transcriptomic analysis 101 RNA preparation from infected cells was performed as previously described (14). 102 Briefly, bank vole cells were infected with orthohantaviruses at a multiplicity of 103 5 infection (MOI) of 0.5. Total RNA was extracted 5 days post infection (dpi). After 104 washing with PBS, cells were treated with Trizol (Tri Reagent, Sigma Aldrich) and 105 chloroform. The aqueous phase containing the RNA was precipitated with 106 isopropanol and resuspended in distilled water. RNA concentration was measured 107 using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific). Four biological replicates 108 were generated for each condition: non-infected controls (NI) and cells infected with 109 PUUV, PHV or TULV orthohantaviruses. 110 Strand-specific single-end cDNA libraries were prepared from total RNA using 111 the Illumina Stranded mRNA prep, ligation preparation kit (Illumina) according to the 112 manufacturer’s instructions. Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 113 platform. 114 RNA-seq analyses were performed using the Sequana framework, v0.14.1 (20). 115 Viral infection in samples was first verified using the Sequana mapper workflow to 116 detect specific viral RNA sequences. Transcriptomic analysis was conducted using 117 the Sequana RNA-seq pipeline (v0.15.2), implemented in Snakemake (21) and 118 available at https://github.com/sequana/sequana_RNA-seq, using default 119 parameters. Adapter trimming and quality filtering were performed with fastp v0.20.1 120 (22). Cleaned reads were aligned with STAR (23) against the Myodes glareolus 121 reference genome assembly GCA_902806735.1 and the Mus musculus reference 122 genome (GRCm38/mm10). Library strandedness was automatically inferred by the 123 pipeline, and gene-level counts were generated using FeatureCounts (package 124 Subread v2.0.1). Differential gene expression analysis was performed from the count 125 matrix using DESeq2 (v1.38.2) with R v4.2.1. Statistical significance was assessed 126 using Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-values with a false discovery rate (FDR) 127 threshold of 0.05. 128 6 All third-party software dependencies were executed within containerized 129 environments provided through the Damona project (https://damona.readthedocs.io), 130 ensuring reproducibility. 131 Visualization of differentially expressed genes 132 Venn diagrams were drawn using the online Venny 2.1 program, an interactive tool 133 for comparing lists with Venn's diagrams (24) allowing the determination of the 134 number and identification of genes common or specific to a given situation. Volcano 135 plots and gene comparison representations were obtained using GraphPad Prism 11. 136 Heatmaps representations of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were 137 generated using the pheatmap function in the R program. This analysis was 138 performed for tracheal cells infected with PUUV, PHV, or TULV across the bank vole 139 and mouse reference genomes (BV and mm10). For each condition, only one entry 140 per gene was retained, prioritizing the lowest adjusted p-value (padj) and, in case of 141 ties, the largest absolute log2FoldChange. For the relative representation of genes 142 identified through the BV genome in comparison to the mm10 genome specifically in 143 infected tracheal cells, the six DEGs tables were merged by gene union, with missing 144 values replaced by zero. Genes with non-finite values (NA, NaN, Inf) or zero variance 145 across conditions were removed. Up and downregulated genes were defined based 146 on the sign of the mean log2FoldChange across the six conditions. Heatmaps were 147 generated using pheatmap in R, scaling values by gene (scale = "row"), clustering 148 columns using Euclidean distance and complete linkage, and annotating columns by 149 virus and genome. This approach enabled visualization of global expression profiles 150 and comparison of regulatory patterns across viruses and genomes. 151 Pathway enrichment 152 7 Functional enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) was 153 performed using DAVID Bioinformatics Resources v6.8 154 (https://davidbioinformatics.nih.gov/tools.jsp) (Database for Annotation, Visualization 155 and Integrated Discovery (25). Official gene symbols were submitted for annotation 156 clustering and enrichment analyses of Gene Ontology (GO) terms, KEGG and 157 Reactome pathways, and InterPro protein domains. The background dataset was set 158 to the entire Mus musculus genome, and Enriched terms were considered 159 statistically significant based on a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value < 0.05. 160 Data availability 161 The RNA-seq data set 1 was published in (14) with accession GSE198751. The 162 RNA-seq data set 2 and 3 were deposited to ENA (accession E-MTAB-16656). 163 164 Results 165 Quantitative gene regulation in kidney cells or in respiratory cells varies 166 depending on orthohantavirus species 167 To evaluate the effect of orthohantavirus infection on gene expression, different 168 epithelial bank vole (BV) cell lines derived from organs targeted by these viruses, 169 such as the respiratory tract (MyglaSWTrach and MyglaAEC#2) and the kidneys 170 (MyglaSWRecB), were infected at a MOI of 0.5 with PUUV, TULV or PHV and their 171 RNAs extracted five days post infection (5 dpi). At this time point, the viral replication 172 of PUUV and PHV is clearly detectable and constitutes a suitable basis for the 173 quantitative and qualitative characterization of gene expression by RNA-seq, as 174 previously described (14). The experimental approach is schematized in Figure 1. 175 The RNA-seq generated a similar number of reads (20-30 million) to each sample 176 and these samples are clustered according to infection status distinguishing 177 8 uninfected and infected conditions (Fig. SD1). The number of identified genes 178 significantly upregulated and downregulated (FC>2 and <-2, p-value <0.05), varied 179 according to the virus and cell types (Table 1). Venn diagrams illustrate, in addition to 180 the number of genes, the percentage of genes specific or common to different 181 situations. Since few genes were upregulated upon orthohantavirus infection of 182 pulmonary alveolar MyglaAEC#2 cells (Table 1), they were not included in Venn 183 diagrams and volcano plot representations. Around 70% of differentially expressed 184 genes (DEGs), were upregulated and 30% were downregulated. However, more 185 genes appeared differentially expressed (DE) in the infected tracheal cells than in the 186 kidney cells, both with PUUV (308 vs 66, Fig. 2A) and PHV (545 vs 254, Fig. 2B). 187 Strikingly, few DEGs were common to these two cell lines upon PUUV infection 188 (1.1%) or PHV infection (8.1%). In the case of TULV (Table 1) very few genes were 189 DE in MyglaSWRecB compared to what is seen in MyglaSWTrach (4 vs 509). 190 While TULV did not induce significant gene regulation in the kidney cell line, 191 PUUV and PHV did (Fig. 3A). Indeed, in MyglaSWRecB cells, 37 of 66 genes (56%) 192 were specifically regulated by PUUV, and 226 of 254 genes (88.9.%) by PHV. This 193 represented 12.5% and 76.6% of the total identified genes for PUUV and PHV 194 respectively, when only 9.5% of genes were common to PUUV- and PHV-infected 195 cells. In the tracheal cells, MyglaSWTrach, the situation was quite different (Fig 3B). 196 Many more genes were DE upon infection with the nonpathogenic orthohantaviruses, 197 PHV (545) and TULV (509), than with PUUV (308). Among these genes, only 10.5% 198 were specific to PUUV infection, 21.6% to PHV infection and 15.4% to TULV 199 infection. Interestingly, in this cell line, a higher proportion of DEGs was shared 200 following infection with all three orthohantaviruses (21.2%) or with the non- 201 pathogenic heterologous orthohantaviruses PHV and TULV (23.7%). In contrast, 202 9 fewer genes were common to PUUV and PHV or PUUV and TULV (3.1% and 4;6% 203 respectively). Although the volcano plots show gene expression levels 204 (log2FoldChange) and their significance (-log10_adjusted p-value), it should be noted 205 that more genes were upregulated than downregulated in each situation (Fig. 3C). 206 Due to the limited information available for the bank vole genome, our previous 207 work identified DEGs in infected renal cells from the mouse database (mm10). 208 Therefore, the RNA-seq data generated in the present study were also analyzed 209 against this mouse database. The percentage of DEGs found in infected tracheal 210 (Fig. SD2A) or renal (Fig. SD3A) cells, specific or common to different viruses was 211 similar, whether using the bank vole or the mouse reference genome. However, it is 212 worth noting that for PUUV, PHV and TULV, only about 20% of the identified genes in 213 MyglaSWTrach cells were found with the two genomes (Fig. SD2B), highlighting the 214 importance of combining the two analyses. The same observation was made for the 215 renal cells (Fig. SD3B), where an even smaller percentage of genes appeared 216 common to the two databases. This result should nevertheless be viewed with 217 caution due to the small number of DEGs identified after PUUV infection of 218 MyglaSWRecB cells. Therefore, all the annotated genes found in the mouse and vole 219 reference genomes were compiled into a single list of identification (Table 2 and 220 Table SD). It should also be noted that many genes annotated as genomic loci (Loc 221 genes) have orthologues in the mouse or human genome. This is for instance the 222 case for 25, 54 and 42 Loc genes (FC>4 and <-4), for PUUV, PHV and TULV 223 respectively in tracheal infected cells, and for 7 and 72 genes, for PUUV and PHV in 224 renal infected cells. The putative corresponding names of these identified sequences 225 have been added to the tables (in blue) and when several sequences referred to a 226 similar orthologue, only the one with the highest FC value was retained. 227 10 Innate immune responses are activated by orthohantaviruses in kidney and 228 respiratory epithelial cells from bank vole 229 We compared the DEGs identified in the renal and the tracheal cell lines infected with 230 the different orthohantaviruses, PUUV, PHV, TULV, using the bank vole and the 231 mouse reference genomes (Table 2). The transcripts regulated by one or more 232 viruses in different BV cell lines (Fig. 4A) were mainly involved in antiviral defense as 233 expected following the recognition of RNA viruses by Toll-, Nod- or Rig1-like 234 receptors (TLR, NLR, RLR) upstream of innate immune responses (12). Only two 235 genes were significantly activated by PUUV (FC>2) in both MyglaSWTrach and 236 MyglaSWRecB cell lines; Ddx60, a helicase promoting RLR signaling, and the IFN- 237 inducible gene Ifit1, known to inhibit viral replication (26). These two genes were also 238 upregulated by PHV in these two BV cell lines. It is remarkable that only a few ISGs 239 were slightly upregulated by PUUV, the orthohantavirus specifically transmitted by 240 bank voles, as compared with the much stronger induction observed following 241 infection with the heterologous orthohantavirus PHV. These viruses do not cause apparent 54 diseases in their natural hosts. Currently, only rodent-borne orthohantaviruses are 55 known to be pathogenic in humans, mainly through the inhalation of aerosols from 56 contaminated animal excreta. After entering the respiratory tract, orthohantaviruses 57 cross the pulmonary epithelial barrier and disseminate throughout the body by 58 infecting vascular endothelial cells and monocytes (6, 7). In humans, an exacerbated 59 immune response (8) leads to hemorrhagic fevers with renal syndromes (HFRS) and 60 nephropathia epidemica (NE) in the Old World (9), or to hantavirus cardio-pulmonary 61 syndromes (HCPS) in the Americas (10). The activation of innate immunity to 62 eliminate viruses, and the viral strategies to counteract it, vary depending on the 63 orthohantavirus species (11). Cells were grown at 37°C with 5% CO2 in DMEM 94 medium (Gibco) supplemented with 10% of heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum 95 (Biosera). 96 Puumala Sotkamo viral strain (PUUV) and Prospect Hill viral strain (PHV) were 97 provided by Andreas Rang (Charité University, Berlin). Tula Moravia virus (TULV) 98 was obtained from Alexander Plyusnin (Helsinki University). The aqueous phase containing the RNA was precipitated with 106 isopropanol and resuspended in distilled water. RNA concentration was measured 107 using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific). Four biological replicates 108 were generated for each condition: non-infected controls (NI) and cells infected with 109 PUUV, PHV or TULV orthohantaviruses. 110 Strand-specific single-end cDNA libraries were prepared from total RNA using 111 the Illumina Stranded mRNA prep, ligation preparation kit (Illumina) according to the 112 manufacturer’s instructions. papers.title_zh: 比较田鼠肾脏和呼吸上皮细胞对不同正汉坦病毒的转录组响应

analysis_zh.background: 正汉坦病毒是啮齿动物携带的病毒,可通过气溶胶传播导致严重的人类疾病,但在其自然的小型哺乳动物宿主中感染通常无症状,并与增强的免疫反应相关。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究对感染了普马拉病毒(PUUV)、Tula病毒(TULV)和Prospect Hill病毒(PHV)的仓鼠肾细胞系(MyglaSWRecB)和呼吸道上皮细胞系(MyglaSWTrach、MyglaAEC)进行比较性RNA测序,感染复数比(MOI)为0.5,采集感染后5天的RNA用于转录组分析。
analysis_zh.results: 转录组分析显示出共同以及病毒和组织特异的调控通路,包括先天免疫和抗病毒信号响应,可能决定不同的感染结果。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究结果凸显了病毒在细胞水平上与自然宿主相互作用的复杂性,有助于理解宿主‐病毒动态并为汉坦病毒跨种传播的潜在监测提供依据。
analysis_zh.limitations: 未在提供的证据中报告

papers.title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak.
papers.abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak

papers.title: Immunogenicity of Hantavirus and evaluation of vaccine protective efficacy: A comparative neutralizing antibody study of vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains from selected provinces in China.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantavirus (HV) remains a significant public health burden in the world. HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) strains isolated 20 years ago have been used in key HFRS endemic provinces in China for HFRS prevention. After decades of effective implementation of comprehensive prevention and control measures, HFRS has entered a stage of epidemic fluctuation at low-level in China. However, the continuous transmission of the virus among rodent host animals may lead to dynamic changes in genetic diversity and immunogenicity of the virus, which may affect the pathogenic mechanism of the virus and the protective effect of vaccines. It is necessary to carry out timely monitoring and evaluation of the immunogenicity of HV. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: A panel of sera was established by screening serum samples from HFRS patients at convalescent phase and individuals who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv. Neutralizing antibody titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and three representative epidemic strains from different genotypes (HTNV: SX26, SEOV: LN03 and FJ-17) were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). HV-neutralizing antibodies were detected from all the selected serum samples. Among HFRS patients, 47.92% (23/48) were identified as HTNV infection, 27.08% (13/48) were with SEOV infection, and 25% (12/48) were untypable. There is a significant difference in the titers of neutralizing antibodies against vaccine strains and epidemic strains detected in the serum samples. For HTNV, both patient and vaccinee sera exhibited significantly higher geometric mean titer (GMT) against vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26 (1:386.08 vs. 1:223.04, P < 0.001; 1:137.94 vs. 1:110.37, P < 0.05, respectively). For SEOV, patient sera showed significantly lower GMT against vaccine strain L99 than against epidemic strain LN03 (1:177.02 vs. 1:297.71, P < 0.01), and vaccinee sera showed significantly lower GMT against L99 than against epidemic strain FJ-17 (1:97.52 vs. 1:243.71, P < 0.001). Significant immunogenicity heterogeneity was observed between SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17. CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: The genetic diversity and immunogenicity of HV, which causes HFRS, have certain geographical regional characteristics. The levels of cross neutralizing antibodies induced by infection of HV from different genotypes may vary significantly, but still provide sufficient cross protection. The HFRSbiv currently used in China could induce broad neutralizing antibody, the cross-protective efficacy might vary against different circulating strains and genotypes. It is of great significance to strengthen the monitoring of genetic characteristics of regional specific circulating viral strains, regularly evaluate the matching degree between vaccine protection effectiveness and epidemic strains, predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks of HV, and timely optimize HFRS prevention and control strategies and measures.

Author summary Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by HV remains a serious threat to global public health security, with its epidemic scope continuing to expand. After more than 20 years of application in China, HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) has been proven to effectively prevent HFRS. However, the evolution and mutation of the virus pose challenges to this specific prevention and control measure. In this study, the levels of neutralizing antibodies against the vaccine strains and the current circulating virus strains in the panel of sera collected from confirmed HFRS patients at convalescent phase and adults who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv were evaluated. Introduction Several rodent-borne hantaviruses are recognized as important human pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) primarily in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, which are mainly acquired through the inhalation of infectious respiratory particles from rodent urine or feces. The viruses are distributed globally, and approximately 200,000 cases are reported annually, posing a persistent threat to human health [1]. In China, Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the causative agents of HFRS, and the infection has a relatively wide distribution, with the highest annual reported cases exceeding 110000 in 1980s [2]. Although the annual incidence of HFRS had significantly decreased and maintained a low level in the last two decades, the geographical distribution range of Hantavirus (HV) infection had shown an expanding trend, and the virus presents a more abundant genetic diversity [3]. HV are predominantly hosted by rodents and exhibit strict host specificity, each hantavirus species is primarily carried and transmitted by one or several closely related reservoir hosts [4]. Virus–host adaptive evolution is influenced by ecological environments, host switching events, and gene selection pressures, contributing to the genetic diversity of hantaviruses. Moreover, as segmented RNA viruses, HV possess the capacity for genetic reassortment, enabling the exchange of genomic segments between two parental viruses co-infecting the same cell, thereby generating progeny viruses genetically distinct from both parents [5]. The frequency of segment exchange and the co-infection rate within the same host cell affect the success of genomic reassortment [6]. With the rapid development of laboratory testing technology and the expansion of pathogen monitoring scope, new HV strains continued to be discovered, presenting rich genetic diversity with regional characteristics in China [3,7]. It has been demonstrated that immunization with HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) which contains HTNV and SEOV, was an effective measure for HFRS prevention. HFRSbiv targeting HTNV and SEOV had been licensed for over two decades. Combined with comprehensive interventions such as immunization, rodent control and environmental sanitation, the disease burden of HFRS in China has been significantly reduced [8,9]. However, the vaccine strains used in China (e.g., HTNV PS-6, SD9805, and SEOV L99, HB9908) were isolated more than 20 years ago. Antigenic variation may exist among different strains within the same serotype, and its impact on vaccine protective efficacy remains unclear. Therefore, evaluating the immunogenicity of regional epidemic HV strains, as well as the immunogenic matching and cross-protection between vaccine strains and currently circulating strains, is practically important. In this study, a serum panel was established using serum samples collected from confirmed HFRS patients and HFRS vaccinees for a comparative analysis of the immunogenicity of HV circulating in China and vaccine strains using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). The neutralizing antibody levels against vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains were systematically compared to elucidate immunogenicity differences and to provide experimental evidence for the scientific evaluation of the protective efficacy of HFRS vaccine. Materials and methods Ethics statement This study received ethics approval from the Ethical Committee of National Institute for Viral Disease Control and Prevention, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Study subjects A total of 48 convalescent serum samples from HFRS patients and 28 serum samples from individuals who had completed a three-dose regimen with HFRSbiv were collected between 2019 and 2020 from Heilongjiang Province, which belonged to HFRS national surveillance system. The median interval between disease onset and serum collection for HFRS patients was 14 days, with an interquartile range (IQR) of 10.5 to 19.5 days. Serum samples from vaccinees were collected within one month after the third (booster) dose. HV amplification and titration The HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and previously isolated epidemic strains SX26, LN03, and FJ-17 from HFRS national surveillance system were selected for neutralization assays. All strains were propagated in Vero-E6 cells prior to use. Viral replication was confirmed by quantitative real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) and indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. Virus resuscitation, propagation, and identification. HV vaccine strains (84FLi, L99) and epidemic strains (SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were thawed on ice and used to infect Vero-E6 cells. Culture supernatants were collected on day 7 post-infection for HV nucleic acid detection by qRT-PCR. Concurrently, cell antigen slides were prepared for IFA. Plaque assay for viral titration. Vero-E6 cells cultured for 24 h were seeded into 6-well plates and incubated overnight at 37°C with 5% CO2. After forming confluent monolayer, the monolayers were washed, and 500 μL of MEM maintenance medium was added to each well. Serial 10-fold dilutions (10−1 to 10−5) of virus stocks were prepared in MEM, and 500 μL of each dilution was inoculated per well in duplicate. Plates were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1.5–2 h for adsorption. After removal of the inoculum, 3 mL of pre-warmed (42°C) agarose overlay (mainly 2 x MEM containing 10% fetal bovine serum,2% Gibco HEPES,1% Penicillin-Streptomycin and 2% low-melting-point agarose) was added per well. Once solidified, plates were inverted and incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2. Seven days later, a second agarose overlay, which was identical to that of the first overlay, with the addition of 3% neutral red to facilitate plaque visualization, was added, and incubation continued for an additional 48–72 h. Plaques were observed and counted. Viral titers were calculated as plaque-forming units per milliliter (PFU/mL): PFU/mL = (average plaque count at a given dilution × reciprocal of dilution) / virus inoculum volume (mL/well). Detection of serum HV IgG antibodies HV IgG antibodies in all serum samples were detected using a commercial HV IgG antibody ELISA kit (Beijing Beier Bioengineering Co., Ltd., enzyme immunoassay). Positive and negative controls were included. All procedures and result interpretation were performed strictly in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Neutralizing antibody assay (MN-ELISA) A fixed-virus (100 PFU/0.1 mL) microneutralization assay was employed. Sera were heat-inactivated at 56°C and serially diluted 2-fold in 96-well plates (starting dilution 1:10 for vaccinees and 1:20 for patients, ending at 1:10240), with three replicates per dilution. Each virus strain (84FLi, L99, SX26, LN03, FJ-17) was diluted to working concentration, and 50 μL of virus was mixed with an equal volume of diluted serum. The mixtures were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1 h. Subsequently, 100 μL of Vero-E6 cell suspension was added to each well. Virus-positive and cell-negative controls were included. After seven days of incubation at 37°C, 5% CO2, supernatants were discarded, and cells were fixed with cold acetone and inactivated under UV light. After washing, 100 μL of detection antibody mixture (HV monoclonal antibody L13F3 at 1:3200 dilution and HRP-conjugated rabbit anti-mouse IgG at 1:1000 dilution, pre-mixed) was added per well and incubated at 37°C for 45 min. After washing, 100 μL of the mixed TMB substrate solution was added to each well and incubated for 10 min at room temperature in the dark. The reaction was stopped by adding 50 μL of 2 M H2SO4 per well, and the optical density (OD) was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader. Determination of neutralizing antibody titer and virus typing The neutralizing antibody titer was defined as the highest serum dilution that inhibited 50% of viral infection. The cutoff value (X) for positivity was calculated as: X = [(mean OD of cell-positive controls – mean OD of cell-negative controls)/2) + mean OD of cell-negative controls [10]. Samples with OD values below X were considered positive for neutralization, and the reciprocal of the highest dilution showing positivity was taken as the neutralizing antibody titer. For virus typing, the neutralizing antibody titers against the HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi and the SEOV vaccine strain L99 were compared. If the titer against one type was ≥ 4-fold higher than that against the other, the infection was assigned to that type; otherwise, it was considered untypable. Comparisons among multiple groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). For non-normally distributed data, non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank test for two-group comparisons, Friedman test for paired multiple-group comparisons) were applied. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. These results confirmed successful amplification of all strains for subsequent neutralization assays. Note: The observations were performed at ×200 magnification. (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control cells. Note: plaque assays were performed in 6-well plates (well diameter: 35 mm). (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control. Farmers accounted for 83.33% (40/48) of the cases; the remaining occupations included three students, one worker, one retiree, and three unemployed/homemakers. Ten sera (20.83%, 10/48) exhibited ≥4-fold higher titers against 84FLi than against SX26. Most sera showed low neutralizing titers against FJ-17, with nearly half (43.75%) having titers <1:20 (Fig 3). full_text_sections.full_text: Figures Abstract Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantavirus (HV) remains a significant public health burden in the world. HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) strains isolated 20 years ago have been used in key HFRS endemic provinces in China for HFRS prevention. After decades of effective implementation of comprehensive prevention and control measures, HFRS has entered a stage of epidemic fluctuation at low-level in China. However, the continuous transmission of the virus among rodent host animals may lead to dynamic changes in genetic diversity and immunogenicity of the virus, which may affect the pathogenic mechanism of the virus and the protective effect of vaccines. It is necessary to carry out timely monitoring and evaluation of the immunogenicity of HV. Methodology/principal findings A panel of sera was established by screening serum samples from HFRS patients at convalescent phase and individuals who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv. Neutralizing antibody titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and three representative epidemic strains from different genotypes (HTNV: SX26, SEOV: LN03 and FJ-17) were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). HV-neutralizing antibodies were detected from all the selected serum samples. Among HFRS patients, 47.92% (23/48) were identified as HTNV infection, 27.08% (13/48) were with SEOV infection, and 25% (12/48) were untypable. There is a significant difference in the titers of neutralizing antibodies against vaccine strains and epidemic strains detected in the serum samples. For HTNV, both patient and vaccinee sera exhibited significantly higher geometric mean titer (GMT) against vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26 (1:386.08 vs. 1:223.04, P < 0.001; 1:137.94 vs. 1:110.37, P < 0.05, respectively). For SEOV, patient sera showed significantly lower GMT against vaccine strain L99 than against epidemic strain LN03 (1:177.02 vs. 1:297.71, P < 0.01), and vaccinee sera showed significantly lower GMT against L99 than against epidemic strain FJ-17 (1:97.52 vs. 1:243.71, P < 0.001). Significant immunogenicity heterogeneity was observed between SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17. Conclusions/significance The genetic diversity and immunogenicity of HV, which causes HFRS, have certain geographical regional characteristics. The levels of cross neutralizing antibodies induced by infection of HV from different genotypes may vary significantly, but still provide sufficient cross protection. The HFRSbiv currently used in China could induce broad neutralizing antibody, the cross-protective efficacy might vary against different circulating strains and genotypes. It is of great significance to strengthen the monitoring of genetic characteristics of regional specific circulating viral strains, regularly evaluate the matching degree between vaccine protection effectiveness and epidemic strains, predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks of HV, and timely optimize HFRS prevention and control strategies and measures. Author summary Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by HV remains a serious threat to global public health security, with its epidemic scope continuing to expand. After more than 20 years of application in China, HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) has been proven to effectively prevent HFRS. However, the evolution and mutation of the virus pose challenges to this specific prevention and control measure. In this study, the levels of neutralizing antibodies against the vaccine strains and the current circulating virus strains in the panel of sera collected from confirmed HFRS patients at convalescent phase and adults who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv were evaluated. There are significant differences in the immunogenicity of cross protection induced by locally prevalent HV strains and vaccine strains (HTNV 84FLi and SEOV L99), which suggested that the effectiveness of HFRSbiv may vary in different parts of China. Our findings highlight the importance of the monitoring of genetic characteristics and immunogenicity of regional specific circulating viral strains to predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks for timely optimization of HFRS prevention and control strategies and measures. The viruses are distributed globally, and approximately 200,000 cases are reported annually, posing a persistent threat to human health [1]. In China, Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the causative agents of HFRS, and the infection has a relatively wide distribution, with the highest annual reported cases exceeding 110000 in 1980s [2]. Although the annual incidence of HFRS had significantly decreased and maintained a low level in the last two decades, the geographical distribution range of Hantavirus (HV) infection had shown an expanding trend, and the virus presents a more abundant genetic diversity [3]. HV are predominantly hosted by rodents and exhibit strict host specificity, each hantavirus species is primarily carried and transmitted by one or several closely related reservoir hosts [4]. Virus–host adaptive evolution is influenced by ecological environments, host switching events, and gene selection pressures, contributing to the genetic diversity of hantaviruses. Moreover, as segmented RNA viruses, HV possess the capacity for genetic reassortment, enabling the exchange of genomic segments between two parental viruses co-infecting the same cell, thereby generating progeny viruses genetically distinct from both parents [5]. The frequency of segment exchange and the co-infection rate within the same host cell affect the success of genomic reassortment [6]. With the rapid development of laboratory testing technology and the expansion of pathogen monitoring scope, new HV strains continued to be discovered, presenting rich genetic diversity with regional characteristics in China [3,7]. analysis.methods: A panel of convalescent HFRS patient sera and sera from individuals immunized with the bivalent inactivated HFRS vaccine (HFRSbiv) containing HTNV and SEOV strains was assembled (A6). analysis.results: Hantavirus‑neutralizing antibodies were detected in all sera (A8). Among 48 patients, 47.92% were HTNV‑infected, 27.08% SEOV‑infected and 25% untypable (A9). Significant differences existed between titers to vaccine versus epidemic strains (A10). For HTNV, geometric mean titers (GMT) were higher against vaccine strain 84FLi than epidemic strain SX26 (1:386.08 vs 1:223.04, P<0.001; patient sera 1:110.37 vs 1:223.04, P<0.05) (A11‑A13). analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS caused by hantavirus remains a significant public‑health burden (A1). Methods: A panel of convalescent patient and vaccinated sera was tested for neutralizing antibodies against vaccine strains (HTNV 84FLi, SEOV L99) and epidemic strains (HTNV SX26, SEOV LN03, FJ‑17) using an ELISA‑based microneutralization assay (A6‑A7). Results: All sera contained neutralizing antibodies; 47.92% of 48 patients were HTNV‑infected, 27.08% SEOV‑infected, 25% untypable (A9). GMTs were higher for vaccine strains than epidemic strains for HTNV (1:386.08 vs 1:223.04, P<0.001) and lower for SEOV vaccine strain versus epidemic strains (patient: 1:177.02 vs 1:297.71, P<0.01; vaccinee: 1:97.52 vs 1:243.71, P<0.001) (A10‑A16); heterogeneity noted between SEOV strains (A17). Contribution: The study shows regional hantavirus genetic and immunogenic diversity, confirms broad cross‑neutralization but variable efficacy of the current bivalent vaccine, and highlights the need for continual strain monitoring and vaccine matching (A18‑A21). Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title: Hantaviruses at the human-animal-environment interface: a One Health review of rodent reservoirs, surveillance, and preparedness.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses maintained in small mammals cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Exposure usually arises from contact with infected rodent excreta, so prevention depends on understanding reservoir ecology, human activities, and the settings in which they intersect. This structured narrative review synthesizes evidence on host relationships, exposure, clinical and laboratory recognition, genomic investigation, and One Health surveillance across several regions. We propose three risk-proportionate tiers: baseline readiness where evidence is sparse, enhanced investigation after a credible signal, and sustained integrated surveillance where transmission is established. Five shared functions are scaled across tiers: reservoir sampling, clinical recognition and referral testing, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental assessment, and cross-sector data review. Published outbreaks in Croatia and long-running surveillance in Panama illustrate how the decision logic could be applied, while the 2026 Andes virus cruise-ship event highlights the need for diagnostics and contact management. The framework provides a practical way to plan surveillance with limited resources, but its triggers, workload, and impact remain to be evaluated prospectively.

We searched literature using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, supplemented by Google Scholar, reference lists, and reports from public health agencies. The searches were updated in August 2026. Studies published from 2000 onward received particular attention, while earlier work was retained when it remained founda­ tional to the biology or clinical picture. Searches combined “hantavirus” or “orthohantavirus” with terms for five related domains: reservoir hosts and ecology; occupa­ tional, veterinary and household exposure; serology, molecular diag­ nosis and genomic epidemiology; surveillance, land use and climate; and Andes virus outbreaks and contact management. Terms and combinations were adapted to each database and refined as the review developed. The purpose was to examine evidence relevant to practical surveillance decisions across different epidemiological settings. 2.2 Evidence eligibility and selection Studies were retained when they directly informed one or more areas addressed in this review, including reservoir ecology and host relationships, animal-to-human exposure, human epidemiology, vet­ erinary or occupational risk, diagnostic and genomic methods, envi­ ronmental and land-use influences, surveillance, and preparedness. For specific epidemiological or laboratory statements, we relied mainly on peer-reviewed primary research; systematic and narrative reviews were used to place individual findings in a broader context. We also used guidance and outbreak reports from WHO, CDC, ECDC, and similar public or animal health agencies when these sources provided operational information not available in journal articles. We generally excluded papers devoted only to treatment or molecular mechanisms with no clear relevance to exposure or One Health surveillance, duplicate or substantially overlapping reports, studies with too little methodological detail to interpret, conference abstracts, and non-authoritative web sources. 2.3 Evidence synthesis and framework development Priority was given to primary epidemiological, virological, reser­ voir, genomic, diagnostic and occupational studies, with systematic reviews and authoritative narrative reviews used for broader contex­ tual statements. The synthesis was organized around five recurring questions: which animals maintain infection, where human exposure occurs, which populations are most exposed, how infection can be reliably detected, and how animal, human and environmental infor­ mation can be combined into surveillance and prevention (11, 13, 14). Because the literature considered differed substantially in study design, host species, geographic setting, diagnostic method, surveil­ lance intensity, and reported outcomes, quantitative pooling was not considered appropriate. Findings were synthesized narratively across epidemiological settings, with particular attention to consistency, directness of evidence, methodological clarity, and operational rele­ vance. Greater interpretive weight was given to longitudinal surveil­ lance, well-characterized reservoir studies, linked human-animal investigations, molecularly confirmed outbreaks, and studies with clearly described sampling and diagnostic methods. The tiered sur­ veillance framework was developed from recurring operational needs identified across these evidence domains and should be interpreted as an evidence-informed proposal rather than a formally validated guideline. We considered five dimensions when interpreting a study: rele­ vance to the question; reliable identification of the host and infection; a clear sampling denominator, time frame, and assay; a longitudinal or linked human-animal design when needed to support an inference; and agreement or disagreement with findings from other settings. A serological result without supporting exposure or molecular data was not taken as evidence of current transmission. These considerations informed the narrative synthesis rather than a formal quality score. Hantavirus refers to the group, while orthohantavirus is used where taxonomic precision is required. We distinguish reservoir hosts, in which infection is per­ sistent and largely asymptomatic, from incidental hosts, and we dis­ tinguish serological evidence of past exposure from molecular detection of viral RNA, reservoir infection from human exposure, and human exposure from confirmed disease. Antibody detection in a rodent or a person is not by itself evidence of current transmission, and a positive rodent does not establish human disease risk in the absence of a plausible exposure pathway. One interpretive principle applies throughout: absence of pub­ lished surveillance is not equivalent to absence of infection. Evidence- sparse settings are therefore discussed in terms of surveillance gaps and preparedness needs rather than assumed local transmission or assumed local safety. The distinction matters particularly for neglected zoonoses, where diagnostic capacity and small-mammal sampling tend to be concentrated in a small number of research centers. 3 Hantavirus biology and disease spectrum The genome comprises small (S), medium (M) and large (L) seg­ ments encoding the nucleocapsid protein, the Gn/Gc glycoprotein precursor and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, respectively (15). Genetic diversity arises through mutation, reassortment, pro­ longed host association and occasional host-switching events (16, 17). papers.title: Case Report: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Seoul orthohantavirus mimicking severe acute pancreatitis: dynamic imaging evolution and pathogen confirmation by mNGS.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges. CASE PRESENTATION: A 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology. CONCLUSION: Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome (A1).
analysis.methods: A single 33‑year‑old patient was evaluated (A3); whole‑blood metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) was performed to detect pathogens (A7).
analysis.results: The patient presented with fever, vomiting, diarrhea, profound thrombocytopenia (nadir 29 × 10⁹/L), renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria without typical pancreatitis risk factors (A5). Initial CT suggested severe acute pancreatitis (A4), but contrast‑enhanced CT showed progressive retroperitoneal exudation with mild pancreatic changes and new bilateral pleural effusion (A6). mNGS identified high‑copy Seoul orthohantavirus (A7). The patient recovered fully after supportive care, IVIG, and symptomatic treatment, and pre‑discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreas (A8, A9).
analysis.contribution: The report highlights that Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically, and that disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues; mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation (A10, A11).
analysis.limitations: Only a single case is described and the information is limited to the abstract; broader epidemiologic or mechanistic conclusions cannot be drawn.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a zoonotic orthohantavirus disease with fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak (A1). Methods: A 33‑year‑old patient was evaluated (A3) and whole‑blood mNGS was used for pathogen detection (A7). Results: The patient had fever, vomiting, diarrhea, severe thrombocytopenia, renal dysfunction, and imaging suggestive of pancreatitis but with mild pancreatic changes; mNGS identified Seoul orthohantavirus; he recovered fully with supportive care (A4‑A9). Contribution: The case shows Seoul orthohantavirus can mimic severe acute pancreatitis and that mNGS provides rapid definitive diagnosis (A10‑A11). Limitations: Single‑case abstract only, limiting generalizability.

papers.title_zh: 病例报告:由首尔 正汉坦病毒 引起的 肾综合征出血热 伪装为重症急性胰腺炎:动态影像演变及mNGS病原体确认。

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热 (HFRS) 是一种由 正汉坦病毒 引起的动物源性疾病,特征为发热、血小板减少、肾功能受损和毛细血管漏综合征 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 对一名33岁单一患者进行评估 (A3);对全血进行宏基因组下一代测序 (mNGS) 以检测病原体 (A7)。
analysis_zh.results: 患者出现发热、呕吐、腹泻、严重血小板减少(最低值 29 × 109/L)、肾功能受损、血尿和蛋白尿,且无典型胰腺炎危险因素 (A5)。初始 CT 提示重度急性胰腺炎 (A4),但增强 CT 显示进行性后腹膜渗出伴轻度胰腺改变及新发双侧胸腔积液 (A6)。mNGS 鉴定出高拷贝首尔病毒 正汉坦病毒 (A7)。患者在支持治疗、IVIG 和对症治疗后完全恢复,出院前超声显示胰腺正常 (A8, A9)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 报告强调首尔病毒 正汉坦病毒 感染在临床和影像学上可高度模拟重度急性胰腺炎,且血小板显著下降、肾脏受累以及胰腺实质保持完整是关键诊断线索;mNGS 可实现早期明确的病原确认 (A10, A11)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅描述了单例,信息仅限于摘要;无法得出更广泛的流行病学或机制性结论。

papers.title: Early warning indicators for severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a significant public health concern, and early identification of severe cases is critical for improving outcomes. This review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators for severe HFRS. Clinically accessible indicators form the basis of early risk stratification. Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine laboratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Immunological markers provide mechanistic insight that also supports early identification of severe HFRS, as reflected by a core cytokine imbalance, impaired antigen-specific T- and B-cell responses, and aberrant activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and the complement system. Emerging biomarkers of endothelial barrier disruption, early renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation may further enhance predictive capacity. Despite these advances, challenges remain regarding external validation and clinical translation. Future research should focus on establishing standardized, multicenter-validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS.

papers.full_text: AbstractHemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a significant public health concern, and early identification of severe cases is critical for improving outcomes. This review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators for severe HFRS. Clinically accessible indicators form the basis of early risk stratification. Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine laboratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Immunological markers provide mechanistic insight that also supports early identification of severe HFRS, as reflected by a core cytokine imbalance, impaired antigen-specific T- and B-cell responses, and aberrant activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and the complement system. Emerging biomarkers of endothelial barrier disruption, early renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation may further enhance predictive capacity. Despite these advances, challenges remain regarding external validation and clinical translation. Future research should focus on establishing standardized, multicenter-validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS.Keywords: biomarkers, early warning indicators, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, risk stratification, severe HFRS Supplementary materialThe Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2026.1986264/full#supplementary-material Supplementary Materials 5.Conclusion and discussionHFRS severity progression is characterized by acute onset and rapid deterioration, and given the lack of specific antiviral therapy currently available, early identification of high-risk patients is critical for improving prognosis. This review addresses this core clinical challenge by comprehensively synthesizing predictive evidence from three dimensions, namely routine clinical indicators, immune dysregulation-related markers, and emerging biomarkers. It delineates the knowledge landscape of HFRS severity prediction.Bedside indicators and routine clinical parameters offer the greatest accessibility and constitute the foundation of the warning system. Expert Consensus has identified high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, conjunctival chemosis, and obvious bleeding tendency as severity warning indicators (10). Pleural effusion and qSOFA score also provide independent warning information (19). Among laboratory indicators, thrombocytopenia and leukocytosis represent the most classic combination for early warning (11, 22). PCT demonstrates robust predictive value for severity and mortality (27), while CRP has limited independent predictive value (28). Elevated D-dimer and sTM reflect early hyperfibrinolysis and endothelial injury (23, 31). APRI and ferritin add warning information from the perspectives of hepatic injury and inflammatory burden (7, 40). Building on these indicators, multi-marker prediction models have been shown to substantially improve discriminative performance, highlighting the integration of multidimensional indicators as an effective strategy for enhancing the early warning capacity for severe HFRS (39, 41–43).Immunological markers also play a critical role in HFRS severity prediction. The elevation of IL-6 and TNF-α combined with the decrease of IFN-γ and TGF-β constitutes the core cytokine imbalance signature (49, 50, 52–54). Aberrant upregulation of MCP-1 and CXCL10 reflects excessive innate immune activation (56, 57). At the T cell level, attenuated antigen-specific responses and abnormal expansion of CD4+CD8+ T cells provide warning signals of severe HFRS (64). Delayed IgG responses are also a characteristic feature of severity (71). sCD163, as a monocyte-macrophage activation marker, is positively correlated with renal injury and negatively correlated with PLT, suggesting its potential in the prediction of severe HFRS (74).Emerging biomarkers extend the early warning capacity by encompassing pathophysiological dimensions that conventional measures do not completely cover, including endothelial injury, renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation. SOD and other oxidative stress markers, along with APN and resistin, provide additional warning signals from the perspectives of antioxidant defense and lipid metabolism disruption (98, 99, 101).Each category of biomarkers has its own strengths and limitations. Immunological markers can provide earlier insight into severe warning, but their measurement often relies on specialized detection platforms such as flow cytometry and ELISPOT. Emerging biomarkers expand the scope of early warning, however, most of them remain at the single-center exploratory stage, and their independent predictive value and clinical feasibility still need further validation.Despite the relatively abundant evidence summarized above, the current literature on severe HFRS prediction still has several limitations. Most existing studies on early warning of severe HFRS consist of single-center retrospective cohort studies with small sample sizes, and there has been significant variation in inclusion and exclusion criteria, timing of biomarker measurements, and data collection methods. Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are major causes of HFRS in Asia. Puumala virus (PUUV) predominates in Europe and generally causes a milder form known as nephropathia epidemica (NE), with a case fatality rate of 0.1% to 0.4%. Not all patients experience every phase in complete sequence; phase overlap frequently occurs, in which features of two or more phases appear simultaneously (10). In clinical practice, mild and moderate cases are often grouped together as a broad “mild” category, while severe and critical cases are grouped as “severe” (7, 11–13). full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractHemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a significant public health concern, and early identification of severe cases is critical for improving outcomes. This review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators for severe HFRS. Clinically accessible indicators form the basis of early risk stratification. Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine laboratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Immunological markers provide mechanistic insight that also supports early identification of severe HFRS, as reflected by a core cytokine imbalance, impaired antigen-specific T- and B-cell responses, and aberrant activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and the complement system. Emerging biomarkers of endothelial barrier disruption, early renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation may further enhance predictive capacity. Despite these advances, challenges remain regarding external validation and clinical translation. Future research should focus on establishing standardized, multicenter-validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS.Keywords: biomarkers, early warning indicators, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, risk stratification, severe HFRS

papers.title: Andes virus molecular diagnosis and viral RNA kinetics using a research use only RT-PCR assay: Experience from a Spanish tertiary hospital.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the clinical performance and qualitative agreement of a commercially available Research Use Only (RUO) real-time RT-PCR assay for Andes virus (ANDV) detection and longitudinal molecular monitoring during the first imported ANDV outbreak managed in Spain. METHODS: Fourteen repatriated individuals exposed to an ANDV outbreak underwent molecular screening using whole blood and serum specimens. Confirmed cases were prospectively monitored with serial whole blood, serum, oropharyngeal swab, urine, and rectal swab specimens collected every 72 h. Clinical specimens were inactivated in a Biosafety Level 3 facility before automated RNA extraction and testing with the RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay (Altona Diagnostics, Hamburg, Germany). All specimens were also analyzed at the Spanish National Reference Laboratory using a hantavirus-specific real-time RT-PCR reference method. Qualitative agreement, Ct value correlation, and viral RNA kinetics were assessed. RESULTS: A total of 185 clinical specimens were analyzed, including 124 screening specimens from exposed individuals and 61 specimens collected during longitudinal follow-up of two confirmed cases. All 124 screening specimens were negative by both assays (124/124, 100% agreement). Among follow-up specimens, overall qualitative agreement was 93.4% (57/61; κ=0.837), and Ct values showed a strong correlation between assays (Pearson's r = 0.965). Four discordant results occurred in specimens with high Ct values (≥34-35), consistent with low concentrations of detectable viral RNA. Whole blood showed the lowest Ct values and the longest persistence of detectable viral RNA among the specimen types evaluated. CONCLUSIONS: The RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay showed high qualitative agreement with the reference method in the clinical specimens evaluated and provided timely molecular information during outbreak investigation and longitudinal follow-up. Whole blood may be useful for longitudinal detection of ANDV RNA; however, these findings are descriptive and do not establish generalized viral shedding kinetics or infectivity. Further analytical and clinical studies are required to establish the assay's performance and clinical utility.

analysis.background: The study aimed to evaluate the clinical performance and qualitative agreement of a commercially available Research Use Only real-time RT‑PCR assay for Andes virus (ANDV) detection and to monitor viral RNA longitudinally during the first imported ANDV outbreak managed in Spain (A1).
analysis.methods: Fourteen repatriated individuals exposed to the outbreak were screened using whole blood and serum (A2); confirmed cases were prospectively followed with serial whole blood, serum, oropharyngeal swab, urine, and rectal swab specimens collected every 72 h (A3). Specimens were inactivated in a BSL‑3 facility, RNA was extracted automatically, and tested with the RealStar® Hantavirus‑HPS RT‑PCR assay (A4); all samples were also analyzed with a hantavirus‑specific reference RT‑PCR (A5). Qualitative agreement, Ct‑value correlation, and viral RNA kinetics were assessed (A6).
analysis.results: A total of 185 clinical specimens were analyzed (124 screening, 61 follow‑up) (A7). All screening specimens were negative by both assays (124/124, 100% agreement) (A8). Among follow‑up specimens, overall qualitative agreement was 93.4% (57/61; κ=0.837) (A9) with a strong Ct correlation (Pearson r = 0.965) (A10). Four discordant results occurred at high Ct values (≥34‑35) (A11). Whole blood showed the lowest Ct values and the longest persistence of detectable RNA (A12).
analysis.contribution: The RealStar® assay showed high qualitative agreement with the reference method and provided timely molecular information for outbreak investigation and longitudinal follow‑up (A13); whole blood may be useful for longitudinal detection of ANDV RNA (A14).
analysis.limitations: Findings are descriptive and do not establish generalized viral shedding kinetics or infectivity (A15); further analytical and clinical studies are required to confirm assay performance and clinical utility (A16). Evidence is limited to the abstract (evidence_scope).

analysis.summary_en: Background: The study evaluated a RUO RT‑PCR assay for Andes virus detection during Spain's first imported outbreak (A1). Methods: Fourteen exposed individuals were screened (A2); confirmed cases were followed with serial specimens every 72 h (A3), processed in BSL‑3, tested with RealStar® assay and a reference RT‑PCR (A4‑A6). Results: Of 185 specimens, screening showed 100% agreement (124/124) (A8); follow‑up showed 93.4% agreement (57/61; κ=0.837) with strong Ct correlation (r=0.965) (A9‑A10); discordances occurred at high Ct (≥34‑35) (A11); whole blood had lowest Ct and longest RNA detection (A12). Contribution: Demonstrates high assay agreement and utility for outbreak monitoring; whole blood may aid longitudinal detection (A13‑A14). Limitations: Descriptive data do not define shedding kinetics or infectivity; further studies needed; abstract‑only evidence (A15‑A16).

papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒 分子诊断与病毒RNA动力学,使用仅限研究用途的RT-PCR检测:西班牙一家三级医院的经验。

analysis_zh.background: 本研究旨在评估一种商业化仅供研究使用的实时RT‐PCR检测 安第斯病毒(ANDV)的临床性能和定性一致性,并在西班牙首次管理的输入性ANDV暴发期间对病毒RNA进行纵向监测 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 对14名因暴发而遣返的暴露者进行全血和血清筛查 (A2);对确诊病例进行前瞻性随访,采集每72小时一次的全血、血清、口咽拭子、尿液和直肠拭子标本 (A3)。标本在BSL‐3设施中灭活,RNA自动提取,并使用RealStar® 汉坦病毒‐HPS RT‐PCR检测 (A4);所有样本亦采用汉坦病毒特异性参考RT‐PCR分析 (A5)。评估了定性一致性、Ct值相关性及病毒RNA动力学 (A6)。
analysis_zh.results: 共分析185份临床标本(124份筛查,61份随访) (A7)。所有筛查标本在两种检测方法中均为阴性(124/124,100%一致) (A8)。在随访标本中,总体定性一致性为93.4%(57/61;κ=0.837) (A9),且Ct值相关性强(Pearson r = 0.965) (A10)。出现四例在高Ct值(≥34‐35)时的结果不一致 (A11)。全血显示最低的Ct值并且可检测RNA的持续时间最长 (A12)。
analysis_zh.contribution: RealStar® 检测与参考方法具有高度定性一致性,并为暴发调查和纵向随访提供了及时的分子信息 (A13);全血可能有助于ANDV RNA的纵向检测 (A14)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 研究结果为描述性,未建立普遍的病毒脱落动力学或传染性 (A15);仍需进一步的分析和临床研究以确认检测性能和临床价值 (A16)。证据仅限于摘要 (evidence_scope)。

papers.title: Hantavirus as a catalyst for urgent One Health preparedness in Africa: strengthening the human-animal-environment interface.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that exposes critical gaps in global and African health preparedness at the human-animal-environment interface. Although historically linked to outbreaks in Asia, Europe, and the Americas, recent events, including a 2026 multi-country Andes virus cluster associated with international travel, underscore its epidemic potential and rare human-to-human transmission. In Africa, no large-scale indigenous outbreaks have been confirmed; however, ecological suitability, weak surveillance systems, and limited diagnostic capacity suggest possible under-detection. This commentary examines global preparedness systems and contrasts them with structural and operational gaps in Africa, including weak laboratory capacity, fragmented surveillance, and limited One Health integration. It also highlights implementation challenges, such as resource constraints and workforce shortages. Beyond technical systems, behavioral and social factors - including risk perception, community engagement, and trust - are essential to effective outbreak response. Strengthening One Health preparedness through laboratory investment, workforce training, regional collaboration, and community-based risk communication is essential to improving resilience against emerging zoonotic diseases.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 作为加速非洲紧急一体化健康准备的催化剂:加强人-动物-环境接口。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 是一种啮齿动物传播的动物源性病原体,暴露了全球及非洲在人人畜环境交叉口的健康防备中的关键缺口 (A1);虽然历史上与亚洲、欧洲和美洲的暴发相关,2026 年跨多国的 安第斯病毒 集群显示出流行潜力和罕见的人际传播 (A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 本社论评论回顾全球防备体系,并将其与非洲的结构性和运营性缺口进行对比,重点关注实验室能力、监测碎片化以及 One Health 融合 (A5)。
analysis_zh.results: 尚未确认大型本土非洲暴发 (A3),但生态适宜性、监测薄弱和诊断手段有限提示可能存在漏报 (A4);资源受限和人员短缺等实施挑战被突出指出 (A6)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 作者强调行为和社会因素——风险感知、社区参与、信任——是有效应对的关键 (A7),并主张通过实验室投入、人员培训、区域合作以及基于社区的风险沟通来强化 One Health 防备 (A8)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 本文为仅含摘要的社论,缺乏原始数据或系统性分析(未在提供的证据中报告)。
